quote: Nobody expects to get into the good ones.
why: opens the chapter by reporting an absent expectation as proof the outcome is ordinary, the exact banned pattern named by the rule
suggestion: Ground it in a specific fact instead: "Halstead seniors apply to a state school first, an Ivy second, because that's the order everyone's parents used."

why: a mirrored, tautological half-clause in narration that repeats the word instead of adding information, the litmus test's own definition of a writer's sentence needing revision
suggestion: Cut the tail: "...and Chloe's says middle."

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Interiority of non-POV characters)
why: hands interior thought to Ruth, who is not Chloe, breaking the close-third-on-Chloe POV the whole book is written in
suggestion: "Ruth is quiet for a second, then says that's probably it." (an observable beat instead of Ruth's interiority)

rule_name: Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Pointing at the scene)
quote: the problem is not what anybody at Halstead would have guessed
why: the narrator explicitly signals "pay attention, this will surprise you" instead of just stating the fact and letting the reader be surprised or not
suggestion: Cut the tease and start on the fact itself: "The applications start landing in November, and admissions offices start finding transcripts nobody there can explain."

quote: What's on it is classes, the way a transcript is classes
why: a mirrored, self-referential clause ("classes... is classes") that restates itself rather than telling the reader anything new
suggestion: "What's on it is classes, ordinary-looking rows of them."

quote: which rules out the obvious explanation
why: a trailing "which" clause in narration that explains what to make of the fact just stated, instead of leaving the fact to stand on its own
suggestion: Cut it: "Ninety applicants from one school and no two of them write anything alike."

rule_name: Structure (Mystery lives in characters' mouths, never narration)
quote: The research floors, which are not explained. Two rooms in the sports building, which are also not explained.
why: the narrator directly flags these as unexplained mysteries and nudges the reader toward them, rather than letting the ambiguity surface through a character (as the Duke rep's questions do two paragraphs later)
suggestion: Cut the narrator's gloss and let the list stand bare: "The research floors. Two rooms in the sports building." Let the rep's questions establish that they're unexplained.

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
why: part of a six-turn exchange (lines 11-26) carrying only two attributions total; this line and "Four?" and "Four percent of applicants." all arrive with no tag or beat, forcing the reader to count turns to know who is speaking
suggestion: "'It's on their site,' Ruth says." or add a small beat: Ruth taps her phone screen. "It's on their site."

quote: does not understand what she's looking at
why: routes Chloe's confusion through a verb of cognition instead of rendering the confusion itself
suggestion: "the numbers on the letters won't add up twice in a row" or "she counts the envelopes and gets twelve, then counts again and gets thirteen."

quote: Chloe thinks that's probably right, and it bothers her on and off for a week, and then she stops thinking about it because there's an exam.
why: summarizes a week of thinking and feeling in flat report form instead of rendering a single instance of the thought happening
suggestion: "Twice that week she picks the letter back up and reads the number again. Then there's an exam."
